title: Resolution and the diffraction limit
objective: Explain what sets optical resolution and what it cannot do.

steps.title: Light has a floor
steps.body: Two points closer than ~200–250 nm blur into one: the **[[diffraction limit]]**. Resolution improves with higher **[[numerical aperture|numerical aperture (NA)]]** and shorter wavelength, but ordinary light microscopy can't beat that floor — so 'they look like one dot' may just mean 'closer than the limit', not 'the same structure'.

steps.prompt: Two labeled proteins sit 100 nm apart. On a standard confocal you see one dot. Why?
options: They're below the diffraction limit, so they blur into one
They are, in fact, literally the very same protein
The excitation laser is simply far too weak to resolve
The sample must have drifted or moved during imaging
steps.explanation: 100 nm is under the ~200 nm limit, so they can't be separated by conventional light microscopy — not evidence they're identical.

variants.setup: Two spots 100 nm apart look like one on a confocal.
variants.prompt: Does that prove they're the same structure?
options: No — the two spots are below the resolution limit
Yes, you can conclude they are the same structure
Only when both of them are stained in the red channel
variants.reveal: Below the diffraction limit, separate things merge; you can't conclude they're identical.

options: A higher-NA objective paired with a shorter wavelength
More digital zoom or a higher-power eyepiece
Cutting and imaging a considerably thicker section
Opening up to a much bigger overall field of view
steps.explanation: Resolution scales with NA and inversely with wavelength. Brightness and field of view don't set resolving power.

variants.setup: You need to resolve finer detail.
options: Higher-NA objective with a shorter wavelength
Switching down to a lower magnification lens
Simply using a much longer camera exposure
variants.reveal: Higher NA and shorter wavelength tighten the resolution limit.

steps.title: Beyond the limit
steps.body: Super-resolution methods (STORM, STED) break the diffraction floor with clever tricks, but they're specialized. For most tissue work, know the limit and don't over-interpret a single dot.
